label: the already-sorted fast path is never taken
old: let repeat = if spikes.windows(2).all(|w| w[0] <= w[1]) {
equivalent: `Spike` derives a total `Ord`, and both arms of this `if` search the SAME total order for the first adjacent equal pair. The fast arm scans `spikes` itself and is entered only when `spikes.windows(2).all(|w| w[0] <= w[1])` holds, i.e. only when `spikes` is already non-decreasing; the slow arm scans `spikes.to_vec()` sorted. Two non-decreasing sequences that are permutations of the same multiset are equal element by element, so whenever the guard holds the sorted copy IS `spikes`, and `windows(2).find(|w| w[0] == w[1]).map(|w| w[0])` returns the same `Option<Spike>` — the same spike, from the same position — out of either. When the guard does NOT hold, the mutation changes nothing at all, because both the original and the mutant take the `else`. `if false` therefore returns the same value on every input; what it deletes is the allocation, not a check, and the `ImpossibleSpike` this feeds names the same `(t, source)` either way. MEASURED, by building the fixture rather than by reading the tests: both arms evaluated on all 5,461 spike sequences of length 0 to 6 over the alphabet {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)} — 210 of which are already sorted and so are the ones the mutation moves — gave an identical `Option<Spike>` on every one, zero differences. No test can tell them apart because there is nothing to tell apart.

label: the synapse count and the inference count are supplied the wrong way round
old: let spikes_per_synapse = ledger.spikes_per_synapse(net.n_syn as u64, inferences);
new: let spikes_per_synapse = ledger.spikes_per_synapse(inferences, net.n_syn as u64);
equivalent: `Ledger::spikes_per_synapse(n_syn, inferences)` is `if n_syn == 0 || inferences == 0 { None } else { Some(self.syn_ops as f64 / (n_syn as f64 * inferences as f64)) }`, and BOTH parts are symmetric in the two arguments: `||` is commutative over the two `== 0` tests, the `u64 -> f64` conversion is applied to each argument separately, and IEEE-754 multiplication is commutative — `a * b` and `b * a` are the same bit pattern for every pair of finite operands, which these always are, being conversions of `u64`. So `spikes_per_synapse(a, b)` and `spikes_per_synapse(b, a)` are the same `Option<f64>` for every `(a, b)`, and no `Net`, `Ledger`, tick count or inference count can distinguish the call site's argument order. The swap is a readability defect in `summarise`, not a behavioural one. MEASURED, by building the fixture rather than by reading the tests: 845 `(a, b)` pairs drawn from {0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 97, 1000, 1000003, 2^32, 2^53+1, u64::MAX/3, u64::MAX} against five `syn_ops` values, 720 of them returning a number, compared as raw f64 bit patterns in both orders — zero mismatches. It would stop being equivalent the moment the two divisors are combined by anything other than a bare product, which is why the argument is written from the expression and not from the tests.
